## Conditional Expectation

Work on a probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F_0,\mathbb P)$ with
sub-$\sigma$-fields $\mathcal F,\mathcal F_1,\mathcal F_2\subseteq\mathcal F_0$.

::: {#thm-aap-4-1 name="Basic Properties of Conditional Expectation"}

Let $X,Y$ be integrable random variables, with [conditional expectation](2.qmd#def-aap-2-7)
$\omega\mapsto\mathbb E[X\mid\mathcal F](\omega)$. The following hold almost
surely:

i) **Linearity.** For any $a\in\mathbb R$,

   $$
   \mathbb E[aX+Y\mid\mathcal F]
   =a\,\mathbb E[X\mid\mathcal F]+\mathbb E[Y\mid\mathcal F].
   $$

ii) **Monotonicity.** If $X\le Y$ a.s., then
    $\mathbb E[X\mid\mathcal F]\le\mathbb E[Y\mid\mathcal F]$ a.s.

iii) **Monotone convergence.** If $X_n\ge0$ and $X_n\uparrow X$ a.s. with
     $\mathbb E X<\infty$, then
     $\mathbb E[X_n\mid\mathcal F]\uparrow\mathbb E[X\mid\mathcal F]$ a.s.

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Proof Sketch" collapse="true"}

Existence of $\mathbb E[X\mid\mathcal F]$ follows by applying the
[Radon–Nikodym theorem](1.qmd#thm-aap-1-9) to $A\mapsto\int_A X^\pm\,d\mathbb P$
on $(\Omega,\mathcal F)$. For (i),
$a\,\mathbb E[X\mid\mathcal F]+\mathbb E[Y\mid\mathcal F]$ is
$\mathcal F$-measurable and has integral $\int_A(aX+Y)\,d\mathbb P$ on every
$A\in\mathcal F$, so uniqueness a.s. gives equality. For (ii), let
$A=\{\mathbb E[X\mid\mathcal F]>\mathbb E[Y\mid\mathcal F]\}\in\mathcal F$;
then $\int_A(\mathbb E[X\mid\mathcal F]-\mathbb E[Y\mid\mathcal F])\,d\mathbb P=\int_A(X-Y)\,d\mathbb P\le0$,
forcing $\mathbb P(A)=0$. For (iii), monotonicity gives
$\mathbb E[X_n\mid\mathcal F]\uparrow Z$ a.s. for an $\mathcal F$-measurable
$Z\ge0$, and [monotone convergence](1.qmd#thm-aap-1-15) yields
$\int_A Z\,d\mathbb P=\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_A X_n\,d\mathbb P=\int_A X\,d\mathbb P$
for every $A\in\mathcal F$.

:::

::: {#thm-aap-4-2 name="Conditioning Known Random Variables"}

If $X$ is $\mathcal F$-measurable ($X\in\mathcal F$) and $\mathbb E|X|<\infty$,
then

$$
\mathbb E[X\mid\mathcal F]=X
\qquad\text{a.s.}
$$

More generally, if $X\in\mathcal F$ and $\mathbb E|Y|,\mathbb E|XY|<\infty$,
then $\mathbb E[XY\mid\mathcal F]=X\,\mathbb E[Y\mid\mathcal F]$ a.s.

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Proof Sketch" collapse="true"}

The random variable $X$ itself satisfies both conditions of
[conditional expectation](2.qmd#def-aap-2-7): $X$ is $\mathcal F$-measurable
and $\int_A X\,d\mathbb P=\int_A X\,d\mathbb P$ for every $A\in\mathcal F$, so
$\mathbb E[X\mid\mathcal F](\omega)=X(\omega)$ for a.e. $\omega$. For the
pull-out rule, $X=\mathbf 1_B$ ($B\in\mathcal F$) follows from
$\int_A\mathbf 1_B Y\,d\mathbb P=\int_{A\cap B}\mathbb E[Y\mid\mathcal F]\,d\mathbb P=\int_A\mathbf 1_B\mathbb E[Y\mid\mathcal F]\,d\mathbb P$,
and the general case follows by linearity, @thm-aap-4-1(iii), and splitting into
positive and negative parts.

:::

::: {#thm-aap-4-3 name="Conditioning Under Independence"}

If $X$ is independent of $\mathcal F$ (i.e., $\sigma(X)\perp\!\!\!\perp\mathcal F$)
and $\mathbb E|X|<\infty$, then

$$
\mathbb E[X\mid\mathcal F]=\mathbb E[X]
\qquad\text{a.s.}
$$

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Proof Sketch" collapse="true"}

The constant random variable $c(\omega)=\mathbb E[X]$ is $\mathcal F$-measurable.
For every $A\in\mathcal F$, $\sigma(X)\perp\!\!\!\perp\mathcal F$ implies that
$X$ and $\mathbf 1_A$ are independent (when $\mathbb P(A)>0$,
$\mathbb E[X\mid A]=\mathbb E[X]$), so by
[product expectation](2.qmd#thm-aap-2-3),

$$
\int_A X\,d\mathbb P
=\mathbb E[X\mathbf 1_A]
=\mathbb E[X]\,\mathbb P(A)
=\int_A\mathbb E[X]\,d\mathbb P.
$$

By uniqueness in [Kolmogorov's definition](2.qmd#def-aap-2-7),
$\mathbb E[X\mid\mathcal F]=\mathbb E[X]$ a.s.

:::

::: {#thm-aap-4-4 name="Tower Property and Conditional Jensen's Inequality"}

Let $X$ be an integrable random variable.

i) **Tower property.** If $\mathcal F_1\subseteq\mathcal F_2$, then

   $$
   \mathbb E\bigl[\mathbb E[X\mid\mathcal F_2]\bigm|\mathcal F_1\bigr]
   =\mathbb E[X\mid\mathcal F_1]
   =\mathbb E\bigl[\mathbb E[X\mid\mathcal F_1]\bigm|\mathcal F_2\bigr]
   \qquad\text{a.s.}
   $$

   In particular, $\mathbb E\bigl[\mathbb E[X\mid\mathcal F]\bigr]=\mathbb E[X]$.

ii) **Conditional Jensen's inequality.** If $\varphi:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ is
    convex and $\mathbb E|\varphi(X)|<\infty$, then

    $$
    \varphi\bigl(\mathbb E[X\mid\mathcal F]\bigr)
    \le\mathbb E[\varphi(X)\mid\mathcal F]
    \qquad\text{a.s.}
    $$

    In particular, $\|\mathbb E[X\mid\mathcal F]\|_p\le\|X\|_p$ for all
    $1\le p<\infty$.

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Proof Sketch" collapse="true"}

In (i), the first equality holds because every $A\in\mathcal F_1$ also lies in
$\mathcal F_2$, so $\int_A\mathbb E[X\mid\mathcal F_2]\,d\mathbb P=\int_A X\,d\mathbb P$;
the second holds by @thm-aap-4-2 since $\mathbb E[X\mid\mathcal F_1]\in\mathcal F_2$.

In (ii), write $\varphi(x)=\sup_{q\in\mathbb Q}L_q(x)$ as the supremum of
supporting lines $L_q(x)=\varphi(q)+\varphi'_+(q)(x-q)$ at rational points. By
@thm-aap-4-1, $\mathbb E[\varphi(X)\mid\mathcal F]\ge\mathbb E[L_q(X)\mid\mathcal F]=L_q(\mathbb E[X\mid\mathcal F])$
a.s. for each $q\in\mathbb Q$, and taking the countable supremum gives the
bound.

:::

## Filtrations and Martingales

::: {#def-aap-4-1 name="Filtration and Adapted Process"}

A **filtration** on $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ is an increasing sequence
of sub-$\sigma$-fields

$$
\mathcal F_0\subseteq\mathcal F_1\subseteq\mathcal F_2\subseteq\cdots\subseteq\mathcal F,
$$

with $\mathcal F_\infty=\sigma\bigl(\bigcup_{n=0}^\infty\mathcal F_n\bigr)$. A
sequence $\{X_n\}_{n\ge0}$ is **adapted** to $\{\mathcal F_n\}$ if $X_n\in\mathcal F_n$
for every $n\ge0$, and $\{H_n\}_{n\ge1}$ is **predictable** if
$H_n\in\mathcal F_{n-1}$ for every $n\ge1$.

:::

::: {#def-aap-4-2 name="Martingale, Submartingale, and Supermartingale"}

A process $\{X_n\}_{n\ge0}$ is a **martingale** with respect to
$\{\mathcal F_n\}_{n\ge0}$ if:

i) $X_n$ is adapted to $\mathcal F_n$ for every $n\ge0$.

ii) $\mathbb E|X_n|<\infty$ for every $n\ge0$.

iii) $\mathbb E[X_{n+1}\mid\mathcal F_n]=X_n$ a.s. for every $n\ge0$.

Replacing (iii) by $\mathbb E[X_{n+1}\mid\mathcal F_n]\ge X_n$ a.s. defines a
**submartingale** (so $\mathbb E X_n$ is nondecreasing), and replacing it by
$\mathbb E[X_{n+1}\mid\mathcal F_n]\le X_n$ a.s. defines a **supermartingale**
(so $\mathbb E X_n$ is nonincreasing).

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Example: Canonical Martingales" collapse="true"}

- **Random walk:** If $\xi_1,\xi_2,\ldots$ are independent with
  $\mathbb E\xi_k=0$, $\mathcal F_n=\sigma(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_n)$, and
  $S_n=\sum_{k=1}^n\xi_k$ ($S_0=0$), then $\{S_n\}$ is a martingale by
  @thm-aap-4-2 and @thm-aap-4-3; if $\operatorname{Var}(\xi_k)=\sigma_k^2<\infty$,
  then $S_n^2-\sum_{k=1}^n\sigma_k^2$ is also a martingale.
- **Product martingale:** If $\xi_1,\xi_2,\ldots\ge0$ are independent with
  $\mathbb E\xi_k=1$, then $M_n=\prod_{k=1}^n\xi_k$ ($M_0=1$) is a nonnegative
  martingale.
- **Doob's martingale:** For any $X\in L^1$ and filtration $\{\mathcal F_n\}$,
  $X_n=\mathbb E[X\mid\mathcal F_n]$ is a martingale by @thm-aap-4-4(i).

:::

## Martingale Transforms and Stopping Times

::: {#def-aap-4-3 name="Martingale Transform"}

For adapted $\{X_n\}_{n\ge0}$ and predictable $\{H_n\}_{n\ge1}$, the
**martingale transform** is $(H\cdot X)_0=0$ and

$$
(H\cdot X)_n=\sum_{m=1}^n H_m(X_m-X_{m-1}),
\qquad n\ge1.
$$

:::

::: {#thm-aap-4-6 name="Preservation Under Martingale Transforms"}

Let $\{H_n\}_{n\ge1}$ be predictable with $|H_n|\le C_n<\infty$ for each $n$.

i) If $\{X_n\}$ is a submartingale (resp. supermartingale) and $H_n\ge0$, then
   $\{(H\cdot X)_n\}$ is a submartingale (resp. supermartingale).

ii) If $\{X_n\}$ is a martingale, then $\{(H\cdot X)_n\}$ is a martingale.

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Proof Sketch" collapse="true"}

Boundedness of $H_m$ ensures $\mathbb E|(H\cdot X)_n|<\infty$. Since
$(H\cdot X)_n\in\mathcal F_n$ and $H_{n+1}\in\mathcal F_n$, @thm-aap-4-1(i) and
@thm-aap-4-2 give
$\mathbb E[(H\cdot X)_{n+1}\mid\mathcal F_n]=(H\cdot X)_n+H_{n+1}\,\mathbb E[X_{n+1}-X_n\mid\mathcal F_n]$
a.s., which yields the required inequality or equality.

:::

::: {#def-aap-4-4 name="Stopping Time and Stopped σ-Field"}

A random variable $T:\Omega\to\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\cup\{\infty\}$ is a **stopping
time** if

$$
\{T=n\}\in\mathcal F_n
\qquad\text{for every }n\ge0
$$

(equivalently, $\{T\le n\}\in\mathcal F_n$ for every $n\ge0$). For instance,
the first hitting time $T_B=\inf\{n\ge0:X_n\in B\}$ of an adapted process is a
stopping time since $\{T_B\le n\}=\bigcup_{k=0}^n\{X_k\in B\}\in\mathcal F_n$.

The **stopped $\sigma$-field** is
$\mathcal F_T=\{A\in\mathcal F_\infty:A\cap\{T\le n\}\in\mathcal F_n\text{ for all }n\ge0\}$.

:::

## Martingale Convergence

::: {#lem-aap-4-1 name="Doob's Upcrossing Inequality"}

Let $\{X_m\}_{m\ge0}$ be a submartingale and fix $a<b$. Define stopping times
$N_0=-1$ and, for $k\ge1$,

$$
N_{2k-1}=\inf\{m>N_{2k-2}:X_m\le a\},
\qquad
N_{2k}=\inf\{m>N_{2k-1}:X_m\ge b\},
$$

and let $U_n[a,b]=\sup\{k\ge1:N_{2k}\le n\}$ be the number of upcrossings of
$[a,b]$ by time $n$. Then

$$
(b-a)\,\mathbb E\,U_n[a,b]
\le\mathbb E(X_n-a)^+-\mathbb E(X_0-a)^+
\le\mathbb E X_n^++|a|.
$$

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Proof Sketch" collapse="true"}

Set $Y_m=a+(X_m-a)^+$, which is a submartingale (by @thm-aap-4-4(ii)) with the
same upcrossings of $[a,b]$ as $\{X_m\}$. Let
$H_m=\sum_{k\ge1}\mathbf 1_{\{N_{2k-1}<m\le N_{2k}\}}\in\mathcal F_{m-1}$. Each
completed upcrossing gains at least $b-a$, and any incomplete final upcrossing
starts at $Y_{N_{2r-1}}=a\le Y_n$, so $(b-a)U_n[a,b]\le(H\cdot Y)_n$. Since
$1-H_m\ge0$ is predictable, $\mathbb E[((1-H)\cdot Y)_n]\ge0$ by @thm-aap-4-6,
giving $(b-a)\mathbb E\,U_n[a,b]\le\mathbb E(H\cdot Y)_n\le\mathbb E(Y_n-Y_0)$.

:::

::: {#thm-aap-4-9 name="Martingale Convergence Theorem"}

If $\{X_n\}_{n\ge0}$ is a submartingale with $\sup_{n\ge0}\mathbb E X_n^+<\infty$,
then as $n\to\infty$, $X_n$ converges almost surely to a random variable
$X_\infty$ with $\mathbb E|X_\infty|<\infty$.

In particular, every nonnegative supermartingale ($X_n\ge0$) converges almost
surely to $X_\infty$ with $\mathbb E X_\infty\le\mathbb E X_0$.

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Proof Sketch" collapse="true"}

For all rationals $a<b$, [monotone convergence](1.qmd#thm-aap-1-15) and
@lem-aap-4-1 give
$\mathbb E[\lim_{n\to\infty}U_n[a,b]]\le(\sup_n\mathbb E X_n^++|a|)/(b-a)<\infty$,
so the total upcrossings of every rational interval $[a,b]$ are a.s. finite,
forcing $\liminf_n X_n=\limsup_n X_n=:X_\infty$ a.s. Using
$|X_n|=2X_n^+-X_n$ and $\mathbb E X_n\ge\mathbb E X_0$ gives
$\sup_n\mathbb E|X_n|\le 2\sup_n\mathbb E X_n^+-\mathbb E X_0<\infty$, and
[Fatou's lemma](1.qmd#thm-aap-1-14) yields $\mathbb E|X_\infty|<\infty$. For a
nonnegative supermartingale, apply this to $-X_n\le0$ and Fatou's lemma.

:::

::: {#thm-aap-4-10 name="Doob's Maximal Inequalities"}

i) **Maximal inequality.** If $\{X_m\}_{m\ge0}$ is a submartingale and
   $\lambda>0$, then for $A=\bigl\{\max_{0\le m\le n}X_m\ge\lambda\bigr\}$,

   $$
   \lambda\,\mathbb P\left(\max_{0\le m\le n}X_m\ge\lambda\right)
   \le\mathbb E[X_n\mathbf 1_A]
   \le\mathbb E[X_n^+\mathbf 1_A]
   \le\mathbb E X_n^+.
   $$

ii) **$L^p$ maximal inequality.** If $\{X_m\}_{m\ge0}$ is a martingale or a
    nonnegative submartingale and $1<p<\infty$, then for
    $\bar X_n=\max_{0\le m\le n}|X_m|$,

    $$
    \|\bar X_n\|_p\le\frac{p}{p-1}\,\|X_n\|_p.
    $$

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Proof Sketch" collapse="true"}

For (i), partition $A$ by the first hitting time into disjoint sets
$A_m=\{X_0<\lambda,\ldots,X_{m-1}<\lambda,\,X_m\ge\lambda\}\in\mathcal F_m$
($0\le m\le n$). Since $X_m\le\mathbb E[X_n\mid\mathcal F_m]$ a.s.,

$$
\lambda\,\mathbb P(A)
=\sum_{m=0}^n\lambda\,\mathbb P(A_m)
\le\sum_{m=0}^n\int_{A_m}X_m\,d\mathbb P
\le\sum_{m=0}^n\int_{A_m}X_n\,d\mathbb P
=\mathbb E[X_n\mathbf 1_A].
$$

For (ii), assume $\|X_n\|_p<\infty$ and truncate $Y=\bar X_n\wedge M$. Applying
[Fubini's theorem](1.qmd#thm-aap-1-19), part (i) for $\{|X_m|\}$, and
[Hölder's inequality](1.qmd#thm-aap-1-11) gives
$\mathbb E Y^p=\int_0^M p\lambda^{p-1}\mathbb P(\bar X_n\ge\lambda)\,d\lambda\le\frac{p}{p-1}\mathbb E[|X_n|Y^{p-1}]\le\frac{p}{p-1}\|X_n\|_p\|Y\|_p^{p-1}$.
Dividing by $\|Y\|_p^{p-1}$ and letting $M\uparrow\infty$ yields the bound.

:::

::: {#thm-aap-4-11 name="Lᵖ Martingale Convergence Theorem"}

Let $\{X_n\}_{n\ge0}$ be a martingale and $1<p<\infty$. Then
$\sup_{n\ge0}\mathbb E|X_n|^p<\infty$ if and only if $X_n$ converges almost
surely and in $L^p$ to a random variable $X_\infty\in L^p$ (in which case
$X_n=\mathbb E[X_\infty\mid\mathcal F_n]$ a.s.).

In particular, for $p=2$, martingale increments are orthogonal,
$\mathbb E X_n^2=\mathbb E X_0^2+\sum_{k=1}^n\mathbb E[(X_k-X_{k-1})^2]$, so
$X_n$ converges a.s. and in $L^2$ if and only if
$\sum_{k=1}^\infty\mathbb E[(X_k-X_{k-1})^2]<\infty$.

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Proof Sketch" collapse="true"}

If $\sup_n\|X_n\|_p<\infty$, @thm-aap-4-9 gives $X_n\to X_\infty$ a.s., while
@thm-aap-4-10(ii) and [monotone convergence](1.qmd#thm-aap-1-15) give
$\sup_n|X_n|\in L^p$; [dominated convergence](1.qmd#thm-aap-1-16) then yields
$\mathbb E|X_n-X_\infty|^p\to0$, and passing $n\to\infty$ in
$\int_A X_m\,d\mathbb P=\int_A X_n\,d\mathbb P$ ($A\in\mathcal F_m$) gives
$X_m=\mathbb E[X_\infty\mid\mathcal F_m]$ a.s. The converse is immediate. For
$p=2$, $\mathbb E[(X_n-X_m)(X_k-X_j)]=0$ ($j<k\le m<n$) follows by conditioning
on $\mathcal F_m$.

:::

## Uniform Integrability

::: {#def-aap-4-5 name="Uniform Integrability"}

A family of random variables $\{X_i\}_{i\in I}$ is **uniformly integrable** if

$$
\lim_{M\to\infty}\sup_{i\in I}
\mathbb E\bigl[|X_i|\,\mathbf 1_{\{|X_i|>M\}}\bigr]=0.
$$

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Why L¹-Boundedness Is Not Enough at p = 1" collapse="true"}

For $p=1$, an $L^1$-bounded martingale need not converge in $L^1$: if
$M_n=\prod_{k=1}^n\xi_k$ with i.i.d. $\mathbb P(\xi_k=2)=\mathbb P(\xi_k=0)=\tfrac12$,
then $\mathbb E M_n=1$ for every $n$, yet $M_n\to0$ a.s. Uniform integrability
is the exact condition that prevents mass from escaping to infinity.

:::

::: {#thm-aap-4-12 name="Sufficient Conditions for Uniform Integrability"}

i) **Domination and $L^p$ bounds.** $\{X_i\}_{i\in I}$ is uniformly integrable
   if $|X_i|\le Y$ a.s. for some $Y\in L^1$, or if
   $\sup_{i\in I}\mathbb E|X_i|^p<\infty$ for some $p>1$.

ii) **Conditional expectations of a single $L^1$ variable.** If
    $\mathbb E|X|<\infty$, then
    $\bigl\{\mathbb E[X\mid\mathcal G]:\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F_0\text{ is a sub-}\sigma\text{-field}\bigr\}$
    is uniformly integrable.

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Proof Sketch" collapse="true"}

In (i), $|X_i|\le Y\in L^1$ gives
$\mathbb E[|X_i|\mathbf 1_{\{|X_i|>M\}}]\le\mathbb E[Y\mathbf 1_{\{Y>M\}}]\to0$
by [dominated convergence](1.qmd#thm-aap-1-16), while for $p>1$,
$|X_i|\mathbf 1_{\{|X_i|>M\}}\le M^{-(p-1)}|X_i|^p$.

In (ii), let $Y_{\mathcal G}=\mathbb E[X\mid\mathcal G]$ and
$A_{\mathcal G}=\{|Y_{\mathcal G}|>M\}\in\mathcal G$. By @thm-aap-4-4(ii) and
Markov's inequality, $|Y_{\mathcal G}|\le\mathbb E[|X|\mid\mathcal G]$ a.s. and
$\mathbb P(A_{\mathcal G})\le\mathbb E|X|/M\to0$ uniformly in $\mathcal G$ as
$M\to\infty$. Hence
$\mathbb E[|Y_{\mathcal G}|\mathbf 1_{A_{\mathcal G}}]\le\int_{A_{\mathcal G}}|X|\,d\mathbb P\to0$
uniformly in $\mathcal G$ because $X\in L^1$.

:::

::: {#thm-aap-4-13 name="Vitali Convergence Theorem"}

Let $\{X_n\}_{n\ge1}$ be integrable random variables. Then $X_n\to X$ in $L^1$
(with $X\in L^1$) if and only if $X_n\xrightarrow{\mathbb P}X$ and
$\{X_n\}_{n\ge1}$ is uniformly integrable.

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Proof Sketch" collapse="true"}

**($\Rightarrow$)** Markov's inequality gives $X_n\xrightarrow{\mathbb P}X$,
and approximating $X_n$ by $X\in L^1$ for $n>N$ leaves finitely many $L^1$
variables $\{X_1,\ldots,X_N,X\}$, giving uniform integrability.

**($\Leftarrow$)** Passing to an a.s. convergent subsequence gives $X\in L^1$
by [Fatou's lemma](1.qmd#thm-aap-1-14). Truncating via
$\psi_M(x)=(x\wedge M)\vee(-M)$,

$$
\mathbb E|X_n-X|
\le\mathbb E\bigl[|X_n|\mathbf 1_{\{|X_n|>M\}}\bigr]
+\mathbb E|\psi_M(X_n)-\psi_M(X)|
+\mathbb E\bigl[|X|\mathbf 1_{\{|X|>M\}}\bigr].
$$

Fix $M$ large so the outer terms are small by uniform integrability and
$X\in L^1$, then send $n\to\infty$ in the middle term using the
[bounded convergence theorem](1.qmd#thm-aap-1-13).

:::

::: {#thm-aap-4-14 name="Uniformly Integrable Martingales and Lévy's Upward Theorem"}

For a martingale $\{X_n\}_{n\ge0}$, the following are equivalent:

i) $\{X_n\}_{n\ge0}$ is uniformly integrable.

ii) $X_n$ converges almost surely and in $L^1$ to some $X_\infty\in L^1$.

iii) $X_n$ converges in $L^1$ to some $X_\infty\in L^1$.

iv) There exists $X\in L^1$ such that $X_n=\mathbb E[X\mid\mathcal F_n]$ a.s.
    for every $n\ge0$.

Moreover, when these hold:

- **Lévy's upward theorem:** If $X_n=\mathbb E[X\mid\mathcal F_n]$ for $X\in L^1$,
  then $X_n\to\mathbb E[X\mid\mathcal F_\infty]$ a.s. and in $L^1$, and in
  general $X_n=\mathbb E[X_\infty\mid\mathcal F_n]$ a.s.
- **Optional stopping:** For any stopping times $S\le T\le\infty$ (with
  $X_T=X_\infty$ on $\{T=\infty\}$), $\mathbb E[X_T\mid\mathcal F_S]=X_S$ a.s.
  and $\mathbb E X_T=\mathbb E X_0$.

:::

::: {.callout-note title="Proof Sketch" collapse="true"}

**(i) $\Rightarrow$ (ii):** Uniform integrability implies
$\sup_n\mathbb E|X_n|<\infty$, so @thm-aap-4-9 gives $X_n\to X_\infty$ a.s. and
@thm-aap-4-13 upgrades this to $L^1$ convergence. **(ii) $\Rightarrow$ (iii)**
is immediate; **(iii) $\Rightarrow$ (iv)** follows by letting $n\to\infty$ in
$\int_A X_m\,d\mathbb P=\int_A X_n\,d\mathbb P$ ($A\in\mathcal F_m$), giving
$X_m=\mathbb E[X_\infty\mid\mathcal F_m]$ a.s.; and **(iv) $\Rightarrow$ (i)**
is @thm-aap-4-12(ii).

For Lévy's upward theorem, $\int_A X_\infty\,d\mathbb P=\int_A X\,d\mathbb P$
holds on $\bigcup_{m=0}^\infty\mathcal F_m$ and extends to $\mathcal F_\infty$
by the $\pi$-$\lambda$ theorem. For optional stopping, summing
$\int_{A\cap\{T=n\}}X_T\,d\mathbb P=\int_{A\cap\{T=n\}}X_\infty\,d\mathbb P$
over $n\ge0$ (for $A\in\mathcal F_T$) gives
$X_T=\mathbb E[X_\infty\mid\mathcal F_T]$ a.s., and @thm-aap-4-4(i) yields
$\mathbb E[X_T\mid\mathcal F_S]=X_S$ a.s. since $\mathcal F_S\subseteq\mathcal F_T$.

:::
